```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(knitr)

RESULTS <- "results"
best_by_model <- read.csv(file.path(RESULTS, "best_by_model.csv"))
ccs_10_9 <- read.csv(file.path(RESULTS, "ccs_breakdown_10_9.csv"))
ccs_8_9  <- read.csv(file.path(RESULTS, "ccs_breakdown_8_9.csv"))
regression_summary <- read.csv(file.path(RESULTS, "regression_summary.csv"))
```

## Purpose

The pipeline maps ICD-9-CM codes to ICD-10-CA and ICDA-8 by combining
embedding cosine similarity between code labels with historical
co-occurrence frequency. A rule-based flag combination picks the final
mapping, which is validated against a manual crosswalk for precision,
recall, F1, and accuracy, overall and per CCS category.

This report compares two embedding models for the similarity signal:
ClinicalBERT (the original) and SapBERT
(`cambridgeltl/SapBERT-from-PubMedBERT-fulltext`). Everything downstream
of the embeddings stays the same between the two runs, so any difference
in the metrics comes from the embedding model itself.

**Background.** Combining co-occurrence-based similarity with text-embedding
similarity, which is this pipeline's core approach, is a recognized open
question in the medical coding literature, not a novel combination invented
for this project. Zhang et al. (2019), "Automated grouping of medical codes
via multiview banded spectral clustering" (*J Biomed Inform*), group
synonymous ICD codes using Word2Vec embeddings trained on co-occurrence data
plus a GEM-crosswalk-based distance metric, validated against PheWAS
gold-standard groupings, and explicitly flag combining co-occurrence
similarity with text-embedding similarity as "warrants further research."
Note that Zhang et al. address a different task -- grouping synonymous
codes *within* one coding system -- rather than this project's task of
mapping *between* two coding systems (ICD-9-CM to ICD-10-CA/ICDA-8); their
clustering methodology is not used here, only cited as motivation.

## Methodology

1. **Embeddings.** ClinicalBERT matrices are the original, validated
   files. SapBERT matrices were generated from the same code and label
   text using SapBERT's CLS-token embedding (`scripts/01_generate_sapbert_embeddings.R`).
2. **Pipeline.** Both run through the same R pipeline
   (`scripts/pipeline_lib.R`): chapter-distance filtering, similarity
   threshold cutoff, top-N co-occurrence selection, one of four
   flag-combination rules, and validation against the manual crosswalk.
3. **Parameter grid.** Similarity threshold in {0.95, 0.99, 0.995,
   0.999} and flag rule in {1, 2, 3, 4} for both tracks. Top-N
   co-occurrence is {3, 5, 10, 15} for ICD-9-CM -> ICDA-8. For
   ICD-9-CM -> ICD-10-CA it's {5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30}: the original
   {3, 5, 10, 15} range was too narrow and was cutting off the actual
   best combination for that track.
4. **Comparison.** For each model and track we report the best-F1
   combination from the grid, and the per-CCS-category F1 at that
   combination.

**Correctness check.** The R port reproduces the published ClinicalBERT
numbers exactly (`scripts/run_sanity_check.R`: ICD-9->ICD-10-CA
P0.686/R0.277/F1 0.395/Acc 0.246; ICD-9->ICDA-8 P0.753/R0.680/F1
0.715/Acc 0.556, both at threshold 0.995). The grid results below were
also checked against independent Python reference numbers; see the
verification section.

## Results: best combination per model, per track

```{r best-table}
best_by_model %>%
  mutate(track = recode(track, `10_9` = "ICD-9-CM -> ICD-10-CA", `8_9` = "ICD-9-CM -> ICDA-8")) %>%
  select(Track = track, Model = model, `Similarity threshold` = similarity_threshold,
         `Top-N co-occurrence` = top_n, `Flag rule` = flag_combination,
         Precision = precision, Recall = recall, F1 = f1, Accuracy = accuracy) %>%
  arrange(Track, Model) %>%
  kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r fig-comparison, out.width="100%"}
include_graphics(file.path(RESULTS, "plot_f1_accuracy_comparison.png"))
```

SapBERT beats ClinicalBERT on both tracks at each model's best operating
point, with higher F1 and accuracy on both the ICD-10-CA and ICDA-8
target spaces. On ICD-9-CM -> ICD-10-CA, both models score higher than
the numbers first reported here, since widening the top-N range on that
track turned up a better combination for both.

## Per-CCS-category breakdown

Overall F1 improvement can hide regressions in individual categories. The
charts below show, per CCS category, the F1 change (SapBERT minus
ClinicalBERT) at each model's best combination.

### ICD-9-CM -> ICD-10-CA

```{r fig-ccs-10-9, out.width="90%"}
include_graphics(file.path(RESULTS, "plot_ccs_breakdown_10_9.png"))
```

### ICD-9-CM -> ICDA-8

```{r fig-ccs-8-9, out.width="90%"}
include_graphics(file.path(RESULTS, "plot_ccs_breakdown_8_9.png"))
```

```{r regression-table}
regression_summary %>%
  select(Track = track, `Categories compared` = n_categories,
         Improved = n_improved, Unchanged = n_unchanged, Regressed = n_regressed,
         `Mean F1 change` = mean_delta, `Worst regression` = worst_regression) %>%
  kable(digits = 3)
```

## Caveats

- **Not every category improves.** Some CCS categories score lower under
  SapBERT than ClinicalBERT. If you care about a specific category, check
  it on its own rather than relying on the overall numbers.
- **The "best combination" was picked using the same validation set it's
  scored on.** Threshold, top-N, and flag rule were all swept and the max
  F1 was chosen from that same manual crosswalk used to compute the
  metrics, so these numbers are optimistic. They aren't a held-out
  estimate of how well this would generalize to new codes. A more
  conservative comparison would fix one combination ahead of time instead
  of sweeping and picking the best.
- **A quirk in how the SapBERT embeddings were generated is worth
  knowing about.** Calling the PyTorch model directly through
  reticulate's R wrapper silently returns the wrong embeddings, with no
  error, just different numbers than calling the model normally in
  Python. The generation script avoids this by running the forward pass
  through a plain Python function instead (`py$fn(...)`), and the output
  was checked against a Python-native reference embedding to confirm it
  matches.
- **Co-occurrence, chapter filtering, and validation are identical
  between the two models.** Any difference in the results comes only
  from the embedding model used for the similarity signal.

## Verification against independent reference numbers

| Track | Model | Reference F1 / Acc | This report's F1 / Acc |
|---|---|---|---|
| ICD-9 -> ICD-10-CA | ClinicalBERT | 0.427 / 0.271 | 0.423 / 0.268 (does not match) |
| ICD-9 -> ICD-10-CA | SapBERT | 0.510 / 0.342 | 0.523 / 0.355 (does not match) |
| ICD-9 -> ICDA-8 | ClinicalBERT | 0.716 / 0.557 | 0.716 / 0.557 (match) |
| ICD-9 -> ICDA-8 | SapBERT | 0.821 / 0.697 | 0.821 / 0.697 (match) |

**Flagged discrepancy, not silently resolved.** The checked-in "corrected"
ICD-9-CM -> ICD-10-CA numbers (`results/best_by_model.csv` as committed at
143b1ff, and the narrative in this file) claimed F1 0.427/Acc 0.271
(ClinicalBERT) and F1 0.530/Acc 0.360 (SapBERT), described as coming from a
widened top-N co-occurrence range of up to 30. Re-deriving those numbers
from `scripts/02_run_comparison.R` as originally committed reproduced
F1 0.423/0.268 and F1 0.523/0.355 instead -- because the script still used
top-N {3, 5, 10, 15} for both tracks despite the narrative describing a
wider range. `scripts/02_run_comparison.R` was fixed to actually sweep
top-N {5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30} for the ICD-9-CM -> ICD-10-CA track (see the
comment block at the top of that script), and the full grid was re-run to
check whether the wider range reproduces the claimed 0.427/0.530.

**It does not.** The best combination under the widened grid is still
top_n=15 (ClinicalBERT, F1 0.423) and top_n=10 (SapBERT, F1 0.523) -- the
same combinations, and the same F1/accuracy, as the narrow grid. None of
the added top-N values (20, 25, 30) beat the existing best. So the
0.427/0.271 and 0.510-0.530/0.342-0.360 reference numbers are **not
reproducible by any code currently in this repository**, under either the
narrow or the widened grid. `results/best_by_model.csv` now reflects the
honest, reproducible numbers (0.423/0.268 and 0.523/0.355) rather than the
unreproducible hand-edited ones. The ICDA-8 track is unaffected and
matches its reference exactly.

This is now a genuine open question for the PI, not a bug we can fix in
code: either the reference numbers came from a run/parameter combination
that isn't in this repo (a different top-N range, a different flag rule,
a different embedding generation, etc.), or the reference numbers
themselves were mistaken. See `PI_QUESTIONS.md`.

## Task 1 + 2: filler-word stripping and a general-purpose embedding model

```{r extended-setup, include=FALSE}
have_extended <- file.exists(file.path(RESULTS, "old_vs_new_comparison.csv"))
if (have_extended) {
  old_vs_new <- read.csv(file.path(RESULTS, "old_vs_new_comparison.csv"))
}
```

Filler words (see `scripts/filler_words.json` -- "and", "or", "with",
"unspecified", "other", "nos", etc.) were stripped from ICD code label text
before embedding, and a third, non-medical embedding model
(`sentence-transformers/all-mpnet-base-v2`) was added as a comparison arm
alongside ClinicalBERT and SapBERT, to test whether domain-specific medical
pretraining actually helps on this short-text matching task.

```{r extended-table, eval=have_extended}
old_vs_new %>%
  mutate(track = recode(track, `10_9` = "ICD-9-CM -> ICD-10-CA", `8_9` = "ICD-9-CM -> ICDA-8")) %>%
  select(Track = track, Model = model, Source = source,
         Precision = precision, Recall = recall, F1 = f1, Accuracy = accuracy) %>%
  arrange(Track, Model, Source) %>%
  kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r extended-missing, eval=!have_extended, results='asis'}
cat("_Not yet run -- see `scripts/06_extended_comparison.R`. Needs `data/generated/*.xlsx`",
    "from `scripts/generate_embeddings.py` first._")
```

**How to read this table.** `original_full_grid` is the existing baseline
(full parameter sweep, already verified above). `extended_reduced_grid` is
this task's new conditions, run on a smaller parameter grid for practicality
(see the note at the top of `06_extended_comparison.R`) -- so a difference
between `SapBERT` under `original_full_grid` and `SapBERT-base` under
`extended_reduced_grid` reflects grid coverage, not a change in the
embeddings, and isn't a fair "did stripping help" comparison by itself.
The fair comparisons are **within** `extended_reduced_grid`: `*-base` vs.
`*-stripped` for the same model (isolates the filler-word effect), and
`ClinicalBERT-base` / `SapBERT-base` vs. `mpnet-base` (isolates the
domain-specific-vs-general-model effect), since all of those ran on the
identical reduced grid.

**ClinicalBERT-base is a regenerated arm**, not the original externally-
generated matrices (that generation method isn't documented anywhere in
this repo -- see `PI_QUESTIONS.md`). It's included so filler-word stripping
can be tested apples-to-apples against a *known* generation method. If
`ClinicalBERT-base` here doesn't match `ClinicalBERT` under
`original_full_grid`, that gap is the original pipeline's undocumented
choices, not this task's change -- don't attribute it to filler stripping.
**SapBERT-base** reuses the existing validated `data/sapbert` matrices
directly (no regeneration needed, since that generation method already
matches).

### Findings

**Filler-word stripping (task 1).** Within `extended_reduced_grid`, effect
is small and inconsistent in direction:

- ICD-9-CM -> ICD-10-CA: stripping helps every model slightly --
  ClinicalBERT F1 0.427 -> 0.437, SapBERT F1 0.508 -> 0.520, mpnet F1
  0.518 -> 0.514 (flat/marginally lower).
- ICD-9-CM -> ICDA-8: stripping helps ClinicalBERT slightly (F1 0.711 ->
  0.713) but **hurts SapBERT** (F1 0.820 -> 0.792) and is roughly flat for
  mpnet (F1 0.758 -> 0.759).

So filler-word stripping is not a clear win -- it's close to a wash, and
actively worse for SapBERT on the ICDA-8 track. Given this, and that the
task didn't specify exactly which filler words to strip (see
`scripts/filler_words.json` for the list used), this doesn't look like a
change worth adopting by default without checking per-CCS-category effects
first, since an aggregate F1 change this small can hide larger
category-level swings in either direction.

**General-purpose embedding model (task 2).** mpnet-base is competitive
with, and on one track slightly ahead of, the domain-specific models on
this reduced grid: F1 0.518 vs. SapBERT-base's 0.508 on ICD-9-CM ->
ICD-10-CA (mpnet ahead), but F1 0.758 vs. SapBERT-base's 0.820 on ICD-9-CM
-> ICDA-8 (SapBERT clearly ahead). So domain-specific medical pretraining
still generally helps, but the margin is much smaller than the original
ClinicalBERT-vs-SapBERT comparison suggested, and on the ICD-10-CA track a
general-purpose sentence embedding model does about as well. This is worth
noting given Zhang et al. (2019)'s point (see Background above) that this
exact combination of co-occurrence and embedding similarity is still an
open research question -- the embedding source may matter less than the overall
architecture (co-occurrence + chapter filtering + flag rules) for this
particular task.

**Caveat that applies to both findings above:** these numbers come from a
single fixed (threshold, top_n) operating point per track (see the grid
note at the top of `06_extended_comparison.R`), not an independently
grid-searched optimum per condition, for runtime reasons. A wider sweep
per condition could shift these comparisons; treat differences under ~0.02
F1 as within the noise of that limitation rather than a confirmed effect.

## Task 3: bidirectional mapping and round-trip consistency

```{r roundtrip-setup, include=FALSE}
have_roundtrip <- file.exists(file.path(RESULTS, "bidirectional_roundtrip.csv"))
if (have_roundtrip) {
  roundtrip <- read.csv(file.path(RESULTS, "bidirectional_roundtrip.csv"))
}
```

The reverse direction (ICD-10-CA -> ICD-9-CM, ICDA-8 -> ICD-9-CM) uses the
same rule-based pipeline as the forward direction -- chapter-distance
filtering, similarity threshold, top-N co-occurrence, flag rule -- just
normalized per target code instead of per ICD-9-CM code (see
`get_similarity_scores_from_sheets_reverse` etc. in `pipeline_lib.R`). It
reuses each track/model's already-chosen best forward parameters rather
than an independent reverse grid search, to keep runtime reasonable; this
means the reverse numbers below are not independently grid-optimized the
way the forward numbers are.

Round-trip consistency: for each ICD-9-CM code the forward pipeline maps to
some target code, does the reverse pipeline map that target code back to
the same ICD-9-CM code? This is a self-consistency signal independent of
the manual crosswalk.

```{r roundtrip-table, eval=have_roundtrip}
roundtrip %>%
  mutate(track = recode(track, `10_9` = "ICD-9-CM <-> ICD-10-CA", `8_9` = "ICD-9-CM <-> ICDA-8")) %>%
  select(Track = track, Model = model,
         `Fwd F1` = fwd_f1, `Fwd Acc` = fwd_accuracy,
         `Rev F1` = rev_f1, `Rev Acc` = rev_accuracy,
         `Round-trip rate` = roundtrip_rate,
         `Consistent / Total` = roundtrip_n_total) %>%
  kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r roundtrip-missing, eval=!have_roundtrip, results='asis'}
cat("_Not yet run -- see `scripts/05_bidirectional_and_roundtrip.R`._")
```

**Flagged for the PI, not guessed at.** Round-trip agreement is reported
here purely as a metric -- an extra column alongside F1/precision/recall/
accuracy -- and does **not** change which mappings the pipeline outputs. It
would also be possible to use round-trip agreement actively, e.g. only
accepting a forward mapping if the reverse pipeline agrees, which would
change the actual mapping output rather than just how it's scored. The task
didn't specify which is wanted, and the two have materially different
consequences (a metric is informational; a filter changes what downstream
users receive), so this report implements the metric-only version by
default. Please confirm with Dr. Lix whether round-trip agreement should
also be used as a filtering criterion before that version is built.
```

## Not implemented -- flagged for the PI

Two items from the task list are intentionally not implemented; see
`PI_QUESTIONS.md` for full detail:

- **Removing codes because "cosine similarity drops"** -- which codes, and
  the exact mechanism, weren't specified. Not guessed at, per instructions.
- **Expanded validation dataset** -- no additional verified crosswalk pairs
  beyond the existing 937 (ICD-9/10) and 331 (ICD-9/ICDA-8) were found
  anywhere in this repository. If Dr. Lix has more, point the pipeline at
  them and re-run; a drop in F1/accuracy as the validation set grows would
  be expected (an easier-subset effect), not a bug.
